text: Instruction pipelining overlaps the execution of instructions. In a common five-stage model the stages are instruction fetch, decode and register read, execute, memory access, and writeback. A data hazard occurs when an instruction depends on a result from an earlier instruction that has not reached the place the consumer normally reads. Overlap can increase instruction throughput, but does not automatically shorten the latency of one instruction. A stall delays dependent work until it is safe to continue.

Forwarding, also called bypassing, sends a result directly from a later pipeline stage to an earlier instruction's consumer, instead of waiting for register writeback. In a standard five-stage pipeline an ALU result produced at the end of execute can be forwarded to the next instruction's execute stage. A load's value is only available after memory access. If the following instruction needs it in execute immediately, forwarding alone cannot make it available in time; a load-use stall is required under this timing model. The exact stall count depends on stage timing and hardware.

A cache stores copies of memory blocks closer to the processor to reduce typical access time. Temporal locality means recently used data is likely to be used again; spatial locality means nearby addresses are likely to be accessed. A cache hit finds a requested block in the cache, while a miss requires accessing a lower memory level. Average memory access time for a simple single-level model equals hit time plus miss rate times additional miss penalty. Cache capacity, associativity, block size, and replacement policy affect behavior.

Virtual memory gives a process a virtual address space. Address translation maps virtual pages to physical page frames using page tables. A translation lookaside buffer, or TLB, caches recent address translations. A TLB miss means the translation is not cached; it does not necessarily mean a page fault. A page fault may occur when a required page is not resident or an access violates protection. The operating system handles the fault. Paging can support isolation and moving pages between physical memory and storage.

Caches and virtual memory operate at different conceptual levels. A data cache speeds access by keeping copies of memory blocks. Virtual memory translates virtual addresses, supports protection and isolation, and provides a process's address-space abstraction. A TLB caches address translations, while a data cache holds actual data. A cache miss, TLB miss, and page fault are distinct events and should not be treated as interchangeable. The detailed order of translation and cache lookup depends on cache organization.

A control hazard arises when a processor does not yet know which instruction should execute next, often because a branch outcome or target is unresolved. A processor may stall, predict a path, or use other control techniques. If a prediction is wrong, instructions on the wrong path must be discarded and fetching resumes on the correct path. These lost cycles can reduce throughput. Forwarding data results helps data dependencies; it does not by itself eliminate incorrect branch predictions.
